findings.issue_text: User email validation with `if: :email_changed?` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?` via a generic EmailValidator from any email-changing path (user updates, admin edits), so `match_count`/`last_match_at` are mutated as a side effect of ordinary validation and inflated on every failed `valid?` call, not just at signup
`match_count += 1; save` in BlockedEmail is a read-modify-write race; concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose increments (use increment_counter/update_all)
BlockedEmail lookup `where(email: email)` is exact-match and case-sensitive, so `Bad@SpamClub.com` bypasses a block on `bad@spamclub.com`; email should be normalized on save and lookup

UsersController response echoes `user.errors.to_hash` and sliced attributes, exposing internal validation structure, and the `blocked` message reveals to spammers that their address is on a blocklist, enabling enumeration/rotation

EmailValidator calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?` with nil/blank values when presence fails, and the blocked-check is skipped whenever a domain error already exists, so match stats are not recorded for blocked emails on blacklisted domains

EmailValidator interpolates the domain site setting unescaped into `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})")`, escaping only `.`, so characters like `|`, `+`, `(` produce broken or over-matching regexes; should use Regexp.escape per domain and anchor with \z
`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` on the create_account_controller class prototype is shared across all controller instances (Ember prototype-array pitfall); should be initialized in `init`

In create_account_controller.js, `result.values.email` is server-normalized and may differ from user input so `contains(email)` never matches and client-side rejection never fires; also any email error (e.g. uniqueness) is mislabeled as `user.email.invalid` when pushed to rejectedEmails
email_validator_spec.rb has no tests for the whitelist/blacklist branches moved out of `User#email_validator`, leaving the refactor at regression risk
blocked_email_spec.rb has no test for case-insensitive matching or for the uniqueness validation on `email`
create_blocked_emails migration has no case-insensitive index on `email`, so the unique index allows duplicate entries differing only by case
Locale string `blocked: "is not allowed."` yields "Email is not allowed.", indistinguishable from `not_allowed` and giving users no actionable guidance

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `match_count += 1; save` in BlockedEmail is a read-modify-write race; concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose increments (use increment_counter/update_all)

adjudication.rationale: In BlockedEmail.should_block?, the code loads a row (where(email: email).first), then does `record.match_count += 1` and `record.save`. This is a classic read-modify-write sequence that is not atomic: two concurrent signups using the same blocked email can both read the same match_count value and then both write back +1, losing one increment. The diff introduces match_count tracking specifically for statistics, and this implementation can undercount under concurrency. Using an atomic update (e.g., update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...") or increment_counter) would avoid the race.

adjudication_records.issue_text: UsersController response echoes `user.errors.to_hash` and sliced attributes, exposing internal validation structure, and the `blocked` message reveals to spammers that their address is on a blocklist, enabling enumeration/rotation

EmailValidator calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?` with nil/blank values when presence fails, and the blocked-check is skipped whenever a domain error already exists, so match stats are not recorded for blocked emails on blacklisted domains

EmailValidator interpolates the domain site setting unescaped into `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})")`, escaping only `.`, so characters like `|`, `+`, `(` produce broken or over-matching regexes; should use Regexp.escape per domain and anchor with \z

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?`, it builds `regexp = Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` where `domains` is derived from the site setting with only `.` escaped (`setting.gsub('.', '\\.')`). This means other regex metacharacters from the setting (e.g. `+`, `(`, `)`) can change matching semantics or even raise a regex parse error, and the regex is also not anchored to the end of the string, so a whitelist like `example.com` will incorrectly match `user@example.com.evil` (since `@(example\.com)` matches as a substring). Both behaviors are verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` on the create_account_controller class prototype is shared across all controller instances (Ember prototype-array pitfall); should be initialized in `init`

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` as a mutable array defined directly on the `Discourse.CreateAccountController` class hash. In Ember, mutable objects/arrays defined on the prototype are shared across all instances, so any `pushObject` (added later in the diff) mutates the same array for every controller instance. This is the classic Ember prototype-mutable pitfall and is fixed by initializing the array per-instance in `init` (or equivalent setup hook).

adjudication_records.issue_text: In create_account_controller.js, `result.values.email` is server-normalized and may differ from user input so `contains(email)` never matches and client-side rejection never fires; also any email error (e.g. uniqueness) is mislabeled as `user.email.invalid` when pushed to rejectedEmails

adjudication.rationale: The second part is verifiable: on any failed signup where `result.errors.email` is present, the client pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails`, and then `emailValidation` will fail with reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` for that email. This will mislabel non-"invalid" email errors (e.g. `user.email.not_allowed`, `user.email.blocked`, or uniqueness) as `user.email.invalid`, losing the specific server-side reason. However, the first part (server-normalization causing `contains(email)` to never match) is not provable from the diff because no normalization/downcasing behavior is shown here; `user.attributes['email']` could still match the typed value.

adjudication_records.issue_text: email_validator_spec.rb has no tests for the whitelist/blacklist branches moved out of `User#email_validator`, leaving the refactor at regression risk

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the whitelist/blacklist logic previously in `User#email_validator` (now removed) is reimplemented in the new `EmailValidator#validate_each`. However, the added `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only tests the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch and contains no examples that exercise `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist` behavior. That’s a verifiable test coverage gap for refactored functionality and does leave the change at regression risk.

adjudication_records.issue_text: blocked_email_spec.rb has no test for case-insensitive matching or for the uniqueness validation on `email`

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail` with `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` and `should_block?` implemented as `where(email: email).first`, plus specs that cover default `action_type`, `last_match_at` behavior, statistics updates, and return value for `:block` vs `:do_nothing`. The proposed finding is about missing test cases (case-insensitive matching and uniqueness validation). This is not a verifiable defect introduced by the diff: (1) there is no stated requirement in the diff that matching or uniqueness must be case-insensitive, and Rails `uniqueness: true` is case-sensitive by default; (2) lack of additional tests is a coverage suggestion, not a correctness/security bug in the code shown. Therefore it’s not a “real problem” in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: create_blocked_emails migration has no case-insensitive index on `email`, so the unique index allows duplicate entries differing only by case

adjudication.rationale: In the migration `CreateBlockedEmails`, the index is `add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true` on a plain `string` column. With the default btree index behavior in common DBs (e.g., PostgreSQL), this enforces uniqueness in a case-sensitive way, so records like `bad@spam.com` and `Bad@spam.com` can both be inserted. Nothing in this diff adds normalization (e.g., downcasing) or a functional/case-insensitive unique index, so the finding is directly supported by the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Locale string `blocked: "is not allowed."` yields "Email is not allowed.", indistinguishable from `not_allowed` and giving users no actionable guidance

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new locale key `user.email.blocked: "is not allowed."` and the existing `user.email.not_allowed` string remains more specific ("is not allowed from that email provider..."), so they are not actually indistinguishable per the text in the diff. While `blocked` is less actionable, that is a subjective UX/content choice rather than a verifiable bug/correctness defect introduced by the code.
